data.title: Mamdani releases 84,000 more 9/11 records
data.description:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani released 84,000 more records pertaining to the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001 following a previous release that showed city leaders lied about air quality. 

“After the horrific terror attacks of September 11th and the devastating health consequences that followed, New Yorkers across the five boroughs demanded transparency from their government — but were met with silence,” Mamdani said in a press release. “We launched the City’s first public portal to make these records accessible to the people who have waited decades for answers.”

In September, Mamdani’s administration released 170,000 pages of records, with the mayor’s fiscal 2027 budget including $34 million to “create and maintain” a portal where the public can access those documents. 

The portal received more than 11 million visits and contained 440,000 pages but Mamdani stated his administration’s work was not finished.

New York City Corporation Counsel Steven Banks confirmed this was the third release of records, writing this release marked “another step toward fulfilling the City’s commitment to providing New Yorkers with an unvarnished window into the City’s post-9/11 response.”

The documents contained city records concerning the air quality in Manhattan after the World Trade Center fell and the government response in the aftermath of the attacks.

The Sept. 11 attacks killed 2,977 people at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and on board United Airlines Flight 93 that crashed in Pennsylvania just over 25 years ago. 

The 9/11 Memorial and Museum estimated that the health effects of the attacks have lingered on, as more than 400,000 individuals were exposed to toxic substances as a result of the attacks on the World Trade Center in Manhattan.

The third release comes after the Mamdani administration resolved two lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch against NYC to release all of the records pertaining to the attacks.

Ben Chevat, executive director of the group, expressed in an October statement that the files showed “a disturbing record” from city, state and federal officials who he believed did not properly address problems and hazards by “slowing down a return to homes, schools and offices, or by better cleanup efforts in those places.”

He previously thanked Mamdani for being “the Mayor, after 25 years, who finally begins to answer the question, ‘What did the City know about the dangers from the toxic cloud at Ground Zero and when did it know it?’”

data.title: Russian ship docked in Libya hit in suspected drone attack
data.description:
A Russian ship docked at a naval base in Benghazi was severely damaged in a suspected Ukrainian drone attack on Sunday, according to Libyan officials.

The Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, was struck by two sea drones while docked in the eastern Libyan port city, triggering an explosion and a fire. An initial investigation found that several drones were launched from a base operated by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, the officials told The Associated Press. Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for the attack.

At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed before two struck the warship. Libya’s eastern-based government said the vessel had stopped in Benghazi to refuel and resupply before returning to Russia under a maritime cooperation agreement between the two countries.

Officials said it had launched a joint investigation with Russia to determine who was responsible for the suspected attack. Russia has maintained close ties with authorities in eastern Libya, using Benghazi as a logistical hub for its military operations in Africa and its presence in the Mediterranean.

The strike comes amid a series of attacks against Russian vessels during its nearly five-year war in Ukraine.

On Saturday, a Russian cargo ship, the Sparta II, was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea, sparking a fire that continued into Sunday. Finland’s military said Ukraine was likely responsible for the attack, which occurred in international waters near Russia’s Gogland Island.

All 16 crew members were evacuated to a nearby Russian vessel, with one person suffering minor injuries.

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo warned that the fighting between Russia and Ukraine was reaching dangerously close to Finland’s borders.

“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo wrote Saturday on the social platform X, translated from Finnish to English by the AI tool Grok. “The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

data.title: This Week on The Hill: Lawmakers break for Thanksgiving as year-end agenda looms
data.description:
Lawmakers are home for Thanksgiving, but they will have little time to enjoy the break before returning to a packed legislative agenda.

With Democrats set to take control of both chambers in January, Republicans have just a few weeks left to push through their priorities before the clock on their power expires. Government funding and a major bipartisan permitting reform bill are among the biggest items facing lawmakers during the lame-duck session.

The most pressing deadline is Dec. 11, when government funding is set to expire. Lawmakers must either pass all 12 appropriations bills or approve another stopgap measure, known as a continuing resolution (CR), to keep the government open and avoid a shutdown.

The lower chamber will also have to decide when to take up a permitting reform package the Senate passed last week. The legislation seeks to speed up the build-out of the nation’s energy and infrastructure. The timing of a potential House vote remains unclear. 

Iran war powers resolutions are another issue to watch for when lawmakers return. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), a frequent critic of President Trump, said he plans to bring a resolution to the floor following his failed effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Senate Republicans blocked a war powers resolution last week that would have directed Trump to end hostilities in Iran, underscoring the partisan nature of the administration’s military actions.

Meanwhile, the White House will keep up its own Thanksgiving tradition. Trump is scheduled to host the annual White House turkey pardon ceremony Tuesday, Nov. 24, on the South Lawn.

What you can expect this week:

  • Government funding deadline looms: Senate Republicans on the Appropriations Committee are saying that a short-term CR is likely.
  • House to take up permitting reform bill: GOP leaders are aiming to take up the bill, which would streamline the process for approving energy projects, after the lower chamber returns from break. 
  • Massie looking at another Iran war powers resolution: The effort from Massie comes as the Iran war has stretched for nearly ten months.
  • Trump to hold turkey pardon ceremony: The two turkeys Trump is pardoning were raised on a farm in West Virginia.

Government funding up in the air

House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) has repeatedly said he wants to push through all 12 appropriations bills, rather than pass a CR, even as Congress operates on a tight deadline to meet the funding deadline.

“A lame duck doesn’t have to leave full-year bills dead in the water. I’ve been actively working with my counterparts to advance negotiations, avoid an unnecessary shutdown, and get full-year FY27 legislation signed into law. With all twelve Senate bills now public and the House measures long on the table, we have what we need to negotiate in earnest,” Cole said in a statement last week.

“The biggest disservice to the American people would be not to try. I refuse to let any opportunity available pass us by simply because some are already looking at the next Congress while this one still has votes to take,” Cole added. 

House Appropriations Committee ranking member Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) told reporters last week that she is in favor of passing full-year spending bills for as many uncontroversial funding priorities as possible, and a “short” CR to extend other funding. 

The three appropriations bills the House has passed so far — funding military construction and the Department of Veterans Affairs, the State Department, and agriculture and rural development — represent some of the lowest-hanging fruit. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is sure to face much tougher resistance — both from Democrats and within his party — when the topic shifts to funding other agencies, including the departments of Homeland Security, Defense, and Health and Human Services. 

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Collins released text for all 12 bills negotiated by the upper chamber this month. But Republicans on the Senate Appropriations Committee said the end result is likely going to be some kind of short-term CR. 

“Everybody’s talking about a continuing resolution,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said last week. “And it may be a resolution with some anomalies to it. That’ll depend, but I’m not hearing anybody talking about actually getting the appropriation bills done at this stage of the game, other than a continuing resolution until sometime in February or March. It’s just the reality of where we’re at today.”  

House to take up permitting reform bill

The lower chamber is expected to take up a bipartisan permitting reform bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), that would make changes to the nation’s environmental laws aimed at making it easier to build projects and make it harder to block them, with either lawsuits or other legal mechanisms.  

“This critical legislation will cut red tape, create jobs, and lower costs for families,” House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) wrote on X. “It is more important now than ever that the House passes this permitting reform bill to the President. Now is the time to finish the job.”

The bill will likely face smooth passage in the House and garner bipartisan support. New Democrat Coalition Chair Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), the committee’s chair-elect Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.) and Environment, Climate, & Clean Energy Working Group Chair Scott Peters (D-Calif.) issued a joint statement last week praising the bill.

“BAAJA will help streamline permitting processes while maintaining key environmental protections to strengthen aging infrastructure and create over 100k good-paying union jobs. The bill also includes the toughest restrictions on data centers – requiring that they pay for their power and grid upgrades instead of passing those costs on to working families,” they wrote.

“We are deeply disappointed that amendments, including the bipartisan Manager’s Amendment, were held up procedurally and left out of this bill. As this package passes over to the House, we will look for opportunities to negotiate changes that reflect environmental and Tribal concerns, they added.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’s spokesperson previously told Politico that the New York Democrat believes the bill “falls short in several areas.” It is unclear whether Jeffries will back the bill when it is brought up for a vote.

Johnson told Politico that he could pass the bill under a fast-track process called suspension of the rules, which requires two-thirds majority support for passage. If he lacks sufficient Democratic support, he will likely have to move the bill through regular order, where GOP attendance issues could complicate passage of the procedural rule.

The bill passed the Senate last week by a vote of 62-33. Just two Republicans, Rounds and Sen. Josh Hawley (Mo.), voted against it. 

Massie eyes an Iran war powers resolution

Massie told reporters earlier this month that he had filed three war powers resolutions aimed at limiting Trump’s military actions in Iran.

“If we just stay here for half the days that Mike Johnson has promised that we’ll be working between now and New Year’s, people have three chances to vote against the war in Iran. The vice president knows it was a bad move. The president knows it was a bad move,” Massie said.

“Literally everybody knows that the Iran war was a contributing factor to the shellacking we took,” he added, referring to the GOP’s major losses in the midterm elections.

The House had previously passed three war powers resolutions. Four Republicans backed the first two, while seven Republicans voted in favor of a war powers resolution that was brought to the floor in September.

Senate Republicans blocked an Iran war powers resolution last week. GOP Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Rand Paul (Ky.), who have voted for previous resolutions directing Trump to end the war, joined almost the entire Democratic caucus in supporting it.

Centrist Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), an ardent supporter of Israel, was the only Democrat to vote against it. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted for the resolution in September, voted against the November version. 

Trump to hold turkey pardon

Trump is set to hold a turkey pardon ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House on Tuesday at 2 p.m. 

West Virginia Public Broadcasting reported that the two turkeys being pardoned this year were raised on Deans Gap Farm in Fort Seybert, West Virginia, by Scott Rightsell and Becky Rightsell.

“Out of every turkey farm in America, the President’s turkeys came from Pendleton County,” West Virginia Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey said in a news release. “Scott and Becky Rightsell, and farm families like theirs, take care of their animals every day in every kind of weather so the rest of us have food on the table. This Thanksgiving, the whole country will see the work West Virginia farmers do.” 

The People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) wrote a letter to Trump last week calling for the end of the turkey pardon.

“It is incredible that someone in the highest office in the land can be conned every year into becoming the unpaid spokesperson for factory farmers—who have him pose beside birds bred to be so fat that they will soon be unable to walk—and get him to declare that he is issuing a “pardon” to these hapless birds,” the letter reads.

The White House did not previously respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Helen Huiskes, Rachel Frazin and Filip Timotija contributed to this report.

data.title: Jeffries faces growing pains with large majority and sprawling investigative agenda
data.description:
Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries is set to take over the largest Democratic caucus since the 1990s, and with it, potential headaches stemming from policy disagreements and sprawling investigations.

Democrats have been in a celebratory mood since exceeding expectations in the midterms and picking up almost 50 new seats in the House, returning them to the majority with numbers they describe as a mandate to pursue their legislative goals. 

Still, the incoming caucus is also historically diverse. And even as most of Jeffries’s colleagues say they have full confidence in the future Speaker, the party is bracing for fractious fights, along ideological lines, and territorial battles over various investigative interests.

“We got a large caucus [and] we’re going to have to be disciplined. I mean, there will be moments. But I’m also going to say to you that our caucus watched the Republicans, and we know we can’t perform like that. We know we can have intense discussions, but in the end, we got to produce because we got two years,” said Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), chair of the Democratic Policy and Communications Committee.

“When Trump got elected, they were sending a message they didn’t like what we were doing. This [election] is an overwhelming ‘They didn’t like what was happening.’ And if we don’t deliver, it’s a presidential election year, they’re going to deliver again, and we can’t afford that.”

While the election of several new members affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) sparked concerns the left flank could stall some policy goals, the party also saw a much larger wave of moderate members win new seats. The challenge for Jeffries will be in balancing the sometimes competing interests of those two groups without alienating either one.  

Additionally, Democrats are promising expansive probes into allegations of executive corruption, with a particular focus on President Trump’s family and administration officials, meaning multiple committees could be competing for the same witness testimony or duplicating investigative efforts. 

One Democratic aide noted that Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), when she was leader, was known to play traffic cop among committees as her staff helped delineate what each panel should focus on. 

The aide said there is an appetite for Jeffries to assume a similar role as “a reasonable traffic cop.”

“Epstein and immigration and corruption — those are right now facing a four-way stop,” the aide said.

“And unless Jeffries stands in the middle and directs traffic on how we divvy that up, and continues those conversations on how that divvies up, it’s just going to be a chaotic mess when committees start holding their hearings or asking for the first conversations or transcribed interviews with whatever investigative targets they have.”

Democrats have already launched dozens of probes while in the minority, but they’ve been almost entirely ignored by the GOP administration.

Several leading lawmakers have not hidden their enthusiasm about their newfound power, which features the ability to subpoena documents and compel testimony — including from the executive branch.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), set to take the House Oversight gavel next year, issued a two-word statement the night of the election: “Lawyer up.”

White House counsel Will Scharf has since penned two letters, one to Garcia and another to committee leaders broadly, making the remarkable assertion their probes could be criminal if done to harass witnesses. He also told Democrats they would need to start over and resubmit their requests for documents once they are formally in the majority.

Underlying that are plans for sprawling investigations with overlapping territory. Immigration is an interest already shared by three committees: Judiciary, Oversight and Homeland Security. 

The Trump family’s profiting off the presidency has also already been explored by multiple panels, and Democrats have vowed to show how those in the president’s circle have enriched themselves through their positions even as Americans face rising costs.

Even the Epstein investigation, largely the focus of Oversight, crosses into other jurisdictions. Judiciary oversees the Bureau of Prisons, and both panels are probing the transfer of Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The correspondence from Scharf foreshadows an aggressive resistance from the White House and underscores the need for coordination and strategizing a Democratic response.

But while some worry the party may cross wires, others say they appreciate that Jeffries has not been a micromanager.

One Democratic lawmaker, granted anonymity to speak freely, noted that Jeffries has avoided “punitive measures” for those who have bucked the caucus, either on votes or in the approach they take in committee.

“I love freedom, so freedom is great,” the lawmaker said. 

“They’ve, especially for committee work, sometimes weighed in, but have been very understanding and accommodating of members as they try to do things,” the Democrat added.

“When leadership has data showing that this type of wording or rhetoric is not helpful and undermines our case, a lot of us listen and take that into consideration. Do all of us bend all of the time? No, that doesn’t happen right now. I don’t think it’s going to happen in the next Congress. There’s going to be people who openly [fight] leadership when they try to tell us to do something, right? Because they don’t like what they’re saying. So that’s going to happen.”

Jeffries’s office did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

Current and former leadership said there will undoubtedly need to be some coordination on investigations. 

“You don’t want to step on your own message. You want to have things relatively focused on what you want to focus on, so that you will magnify the public’s ability to see what we’re doing, as opposed to be distracted by three or four things you’re doing at the same time,” said Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), the former majority leader. 

“Now, will things happen at the same time and just in the normal course? Of course they will. But to the extent you can provide a focus, I think the Speaker will be working with the committee chairs to do that.”

Almost all agree Pelosi was a masterful leader over her many years at the helm of the party.

But Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), who will be the majority whip next year, said he has full confidence in Jeffries.

“We’ve seen his leadership style. We know it’s a little bit different. We served at the leadership table with Nancy Pelosi. She’s amazing. She’s on the Mount Rushmore of Democratic politicians,” he said. 

“But this leadership team does it a little differently, and we look forward to being effective for our members.”

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) said Jeffries will make “a good father in that respect” if any turf wars surface among committee chairs.

“He will  — I don’t know ‘lay down the law’ — but I think he will guide them to constructive decisions,” Beyer said.

“He’s not a wallflower. He’s not somebody who rolls over. He’s very serious, very thoughtful.”

Questions remain over how aligned Democrats will remain as they push forward on policies they’ve promised to combat Trump’s impact on the cost of living, immigration, health care and more.

The Democratic primaries saw several DSA members knocking off veteran incumbents, spurring concerns over the summer that the new “bloc” could be akin to the GOP’s Freedom Caucus, whose members routinely derailed votes and left Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) scrambling to advance even partisan bills.

The election of so many Democrats who flipped GOP-held seats now raises questions over whether the party may have trouble securing their votes on some party priorities that could be controversial in frontline districts.

“There are many times, just from political calculations, where the Speaker’s office has to drive the short-term agenda and the long-term agenda. For example, what bills do we want to take up the first and second week of January?” Beyer said.

“He’s been minority leader, so it’s different. It is different. So he’ll have a lot more power now, and hopefully use it wisely. I think he will.”

Hoyer said for all the new voices in the conference, he feels confident the caucus is aligned on the prevailing issues Democrats campaigned on.

“I think the Democratic leadership is, and I think will continue to focus on the issues of affordability of healthcare, of housing costs, of getting this war ended, and I think that’s what they ought to be doing,” he said.

“And I think they will do it. And I think the caucus is pretty united on those issues.”

data.title: Democrats secure largest House majority in election in three decades
data.description:
Democrats have secured the largest House majority in a regular election in decades, following their notable 2026 midterm election victories in regions where they have historically struggled.

According to Decision Desk HQ, Democrats are projected to lock down 258 seats in the House for the next Congress. The last time the party secured that many seats in an election was in 1992.

Democrats’ wins in this year’s elections came amid an uphill battle for the GOP, with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living weighing the party down as Election Day approached.

In this year’s elections, multiple key demographics moved toward Democrats since Trump won over former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2022. Overall, the shifts were behind an expansive rebuke of the president and Republicans in the midterms.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), most likely the Speaker of the House in next year’s Congress, in a post on the social platform X the day after Election Day, called the Democrats’ results “too big to rig.”

“Thank you, America,” he added in the post.

Less than a week after the elections, Trump, who has a history of election denial, questioned how the polls could have been “so wrong.” He also raised questions about if the elections were “honest” after indicating he thought the results were valid.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump suggested that a number of early voting dumps were “so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote” and asserted “it’s all about the machines” without giving specific evidence.

data.title: El-Sayed would pass Medicare for All as 'TrumpCare': 'I don't really care what it's called
data.description:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) on Sunday said he would pass a single-payer healthcare bill, commonly referred to as Medicare for All, with the name “TrumpCare,” adding that he does not “really care what it’s called.”

NBC News’s “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker noted to El-Sayed that President Trump showed a willingness to work with Democrats and shared on Truth Social on Saturday a social media post where El-Sayed urged the president, who he referred to as “Donald,” to guarantee “healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

“My job is to make sure that we’re advancing the goal to get everybody in this country health care,” El-Sayed, a physician, told Welker. “I ran on three things, money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All. Now, I don’t really care what it’s called. I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed health care in this country.”

He said if Trump was “serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card.” The senator-elect noted that if Trump wanted to discuss it, he was “open to it too,” as well as Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is seeking a bid to become Senate majority leader.

El-Sayed also referred to Trump’s Truth Social post in a statement on Saturday.

“If the President is serious about meeting the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country, I’m ready to work alongside leaders in the Senate like Senators Van Hollen, Sanders, Wyden, and Warren to deliver. President Trump, give me a call. I’m happy to chat,” El-Sayed stated, referring to Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.).

Sanders told The Associated Press last Wednesday that he will push for a sweeping Medicare for All universal health care when he is expected to become chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee next year.

He said that universal healthcare is “no longer a utopian vision.” The plan would implement a universal health care system over four years, lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55 in year one and expand the program’s coverage to include dental and vision care, according to the AP. It would also guarantee health care for children up until age 18.

El-Sayed told Welker he supports the plan, comparing it to public schools in that “everybody is entitled to a public school.” Van Hollen told Welker later in the program that Sanders is looking at making “the necessary changes going forward” with his push.

“But we can make substantial progress going forward,” Van Hollen said. “And Abdul El-Sayed laid out his version. What we’re thinking about right now is having people be able to buy into Medicare if you’re 55-65 years old, to say that kids are covered … So we also need to expand coverage under Medicare. So there are lots of things we can do, and I mean big things, in the early stages.”

data.title: Democratic Rep says next Congress will focus on using AI to improve healthcare, jobs and agriculture
data.description:
Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.) said the next Congress will be focusing on using AI to improve healthcare, jobs and agriculture.

“We can make sure that we do have people overseeing and protecting American interests, American citizens from the risk of AI, while at the same time, making sure that American companies and American technologies are leading the way,” Schneider told host Chris Stirewalt during an appearance on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

He said the Democratic agenda in the upcoming Congress should be geared at addressing the cost of living to make “it easier for people not just to make ends meet,” while also ensuring “America continues to lead on frontier technologies.”

“Using AI to improve Americans’ health care, to improve opportunities, economic opportunities and jobs, to improve production of food and agriculture,” he concluded. “All of these go hand in glove, and that’s what we’re going to focus on.”

On Sunday, Democrats secured their largest margin in the House in the last three decades, with many lawmakers announcing greater scrutiny into the tech industry. 

Schneider leads the New Democrat Coalition, a center-left group of House Democrats focused on pro-business policies. The coalition’s working group has prioritized AI policies, particularly, that “translate into real benefits for hardworking, middle-class Americans.”

The group’s center on emerging technologies will be expected to contend with progressives in the party who are already unveiling plans to relax the development of AI.

Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) said the Democratic party “must make it a top priority to protect Americans’ jobs, freedom and lives from AI billionaires.”

“AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath,” he continued. “Congress should investigate how these companies are putting the jobs, freedom, and lives of Americans at risk. And we should pass bills to protect people.”

In the upper chamber, key Senators are already on board with the oversight push. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who appears poised to chair the Senate Banking Committee, warned Wall Street executives and Big Tech CEOs alike that “accountability is coming.”

data.title: Flanagan says wins made by her, Mary Peltola 'makes our capitol look a little bit more like America'
data.description:
Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) on Sunday said the victories won by her and Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) as the first Native American women to be in the U.S. Senate “makes our capitol look a little bit more like America.”

Flanagan told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union” that she didn’t run to “make history” after Bash pointed to a photo Flanagan posted of herself outside the Minnesota state House wearing a ribbon skirt, a traditional Indigenous dress for girls and women.

“But it is about time that a Native American woman served in the U.S. Senate, and I think it’s important for our democracy that it accurately reflects the people it seeks to represent,” Flanagan said.

“Having an Alaska Native woman and a Native American woman serving in the Senate –– that makes our capitol look a little bit more like America, and I think it helps us get better results,” the Minnesota Democrat said. “And I am excited to serve with her.”

Peltola’s win last week was the final Democratic victory in a sweeping turnout for the party in the 2026 midterm election. She defeated Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), becoming the 56th member of the Democratic majority in the Senate to be ushered in in January.

Flanagan is of Ojibwe and Irish descent, and a citizen of the federally-recognized White Earth Nation. Peltola is of Yu’pik and German American descent.

Both have served within their communities, with Flanagan helped form the Minnesota House Native American Caucus in the Minnesota state legislature and Peltola having been a member of the Orutsararmiut Traditional Native Council.

Several Indigenous candidates won victories on Election Day, from the federal level to the local level. Crystalyne Curley, Speaker of the Navajo Nation Council, won to become the first woman to be Navajo Nation president, leading the largest reservation in the country.

The House saw Reps. Sharice Davids (D-Kan.), Tom Cole (R-Okla.) and Josh Brecheen (R-Okla.) all reelected, with Davids from the Ho-Chunk Nation, Cole from the Chickasaw Nation and Brecheen from the Choctaw Nation.

Reps-elect Clair Valdez (D-N.Y.) of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo and Sean McCann (D-Minn.) of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation were also both elected to Congress.

Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected to be New Mexico’s first Native American governor. She previously served under former President Biden as the the first Native American to serve as a secretary in a presidential Cabinet and the second to serve in the Cabinet. She and Davids were both the first Native American women to be elected to the House in 2018.

Former Vice President Charles Curtis of the Kaw Nation was the first Indigenous member of both the House and the Senate, according to the Senate’s website. He later served under former President Herbert Hoover from 1929 to 1933, and remains the only known Native American to hold such a high office.

data.title: Jeffries says he'll move to ban lawmakers from stock trading 'very early' in next Congress
data.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is likely to become the Speaker of the House next year, said Sunday that he will take action to bar lawmakers from trading stocks “very early” in the next Congress.

“So, well, listen, we’ve got to clean up the mess in Washington. That means the Congress, that means the Supreme Court and that also means with respect to the administration,” Jeffries told CBS News’s Margaret Brennan on “Face the Nation.” 

“And we should begin by dealing with our own house, which is why very early on in the new Congress, House Democrats are going to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock,” he added.

Jeffries’s comments come after Democrats won back the House and Senate in the midterm elections earlier this month, even securing wins in regions where they have historically struggled, like Texas and Kansas.

In late September, Senate Democrats blocked a bill to prevent members of Congress from purchasing new stocks of publicly traded companies, saying the legislation wasn’t defensive enough against possible corruption.

The Stop Insider Trading Act sunk in a 53-47 vote, with none of the Democrats backing and 60 votes required for it to advance.

Last Wednesday, House Democrats nominated Jeffries to take up the role of Speaker, placing him another step closer to being the chamber’s first Black Speaker. Jeffries garnered 251 votes for the role from his caucus, while 11 people did not support him.

Beyond banning congressional stock trading, other priorities for Jeffries next year include reversing Medicaid cuts adopted by Republicans last year and expanding ObamaCare tax credits, with Republicans allowing them to expire at the beginning of 2026.

data.title: Trump blames $6T stock market slide on Democrats' midterm wins
data.description:
President Trump blames the stock market’s $6 trillion slide on the Democratic party’s wins nationwide that saw it take control of both the House and Senate. 

“The Market is down more than 6 Trillion Dollars since the Democrats’ rather strange ‘win’ on November 3rd,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “NASDAQ, by itself, is down 20%. This is 100% due to the fact that the Democrats are ‘BAD’ due to their Anti Growth, and Retribution Only, Policies, and worse.”

“If they don’t change, FAST, it will only get worse. But fear not, our Country will soon be STRONG AGAIN — Lots of good things happening,” the president concluded. 

When stock markets closed on Friday, Yahoo Finance reported it experienced the same drops only seen five other times since WWII – particularly in 2008 and another in 2001. 

The Nasdaq composite, which hit an all-time high in early October, is now in the red since the start of the year. The Hill previously reported as of midafternoon Friday, the index had dipped by more than 4,700 points since closing at a record high of 27,599.886 on Oct. 6. 

Though chip stocks experienced its worst week since the week after the attacks on Sept. 1, 2001, according to reporting from Yahoo Finance. The country’s primary chip-producer Nvidia – which has been hit with numerous scandals over allegations it violated U.S. export controls – has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value since its peak on Oct. 6.

When asked about the market drops, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday its cause could be a “combination of things.”

“We could see that the market sell-off actually began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls and then accelerated after Election Day,” he told CBS News’s Margaret Brennan on “Face the Nation.”

“The Democratic position on the SI [(Super Intelligence)] buildout has spooked a lot of investors in terms of slowing it down,” Bessent continued. “We’ve also seen some very hawkish remarks from the Federal Reserve. Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they over tighten.”

Tech analyst Dan Ives said the rough week for the markets could be attributed to a “perfect storm” heading for tech stocks. That storm focused on fears that Democrats’s sweeping midterm victories would lead to heightened oversight into AI and data centers.

It also included Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, according to Ives. The company is facing multiple probes investigating whether Nvidia lied to investors or violated U.S. export controls.
